subject: WSJ Economics: Warsh’s Shrewd Pre-Election Pause
body_text:
96 Plus, scavenging bankruptcies for AI training data, the price of large residential lots and the public’s trust in the Fed   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Kevin Warsh’s Judicious Pre-Election Pause   Plus, scavenging bankruptcies for AI training data, the price of large residential lots and the public’s trust in the Fed   On Wednesday the Federal Reserve said it was leaving rates unchanged while new information accumulates . What new information? 

   One obvious candidate: Tuesday’s midterm election. 

   Politics were not at play, Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters: “I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”

   But elections can influence your thinking even if you don’t say so. And a central bank can take political reality into consideration without being politicized. 

   The Fed has no rule against moving on the eve of an election, and occasionally has. But if moving isn’t urgent, it would just as soon wait until political passions have cooled.

   The sensitivity is usually around presidential, not midterm, elections. But under President Trump, monetary policy has been politically sensitive 24/7. His circle accused then-chairman Jerome Powell of acting politically in cutting rates half a point just before the 2024 election. (The economic justification was rock solid, I argued at the time .) In office, Trump has repeatedly pressured the Fed to cut rates. He appointed Warsh expecting just that.

   Does holding back on a rate increase compromise Warsh’s independence? Not after he presided over a unanimous vote to raise rates last month. True, that increase was justified by inflation and employment data. Still, if you had said a year ago that Trump’s handpicked Fed chairman would raise rates a few months into the job, I would have called you crazy. By doing so against Trump’s wishes in September, Warsh gets the benefit of the doubt now.

   Had Warsh raised rates this week, it may have outraged Trump, and indeed the entire Republican Party. With what effect, it is hard to say, but Warsh may have lost political capital on anything where the administration has some say, such as future appointments to the Fed. By pausing, Warsh has blunted, for now, one potential threat to his institution.

         And he has done so without compromising his mission, at least so far. That nine of his 11 voting colleagues voted to pause suggests this was not a controversial call internally. Warsh reiterated that inflation is still too high and financial conditions aren’t tight, indicating rates will likely go up in December. On Wednesday markets did slightly lower the path of future rates, but that path remains much higher than before Warsh took office.

   There will be tests of Warsh’s independence to come, perhaps quite soon. This week’s meeting wasn’t one of them.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   Hungry for material on which to train their models, AI companies are seizing on corporate liquidations to buy up dying companies’ data. These moves are troubling unions, consumer groups and other stakeholders , and opening a new front in the battle over how artificial intelligence raises privacy threats. Since the summer, companies including Google have bid $10 million or more in exchange for old emails, operating data and a slew of other information from Spirit Airlines, which went bankrupt last year. Personally identifiable information is supposed to get censored, but the bidding war has generated legal objections from pilots’ and flight attendants’ unions, per bankruptcy newsletter Petition.

   Surrendering to AI: Judgment calls are the main lever through which human values influence AI outcomes, writes Anthropic’s Alex Tamkin . He and fellow researchers asked AI to evaluate a problem so as to lean toward one of several options for action. Human analysts reviewing the work ended up regularly leaning in the same direction as the AI, the study found. “When asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments,” the researchers wrote. “If people defer to AI without noticing, then ‘human in the loop’ might provide less assurance than people expect,” Tamkin wrote on X.

   Smaller lot sizes = more homes: About 90% of municipalities impose minimum lot sizes on zoned lots, write Tobias Peter and Edward Pinto of the American Enterprise Institute. This, they say, helps explain why starter homes are so scarce . Of the roughly 4.6 million homes built from 2015 through 2024 in new subdivisions they looked at, only about 750,000, or 16%, were starter homes, they write. 

   Warsh acknowledged Wednesday that while the Fed hasn’t won the inflation fight, “we’re working on it.” Americans are inclined to believe him . Forty-eight percent hold a favorable view of the Fed , versus 29% with an unfavorable opinion, according to Pew. That split has improved over the past three years despite Trump’s unrelenting political attacks on the central bank. Only the National Park Service, the National Weather Service and the post office are more popular than the Fed. The Internal Revenue Service and Immigration and Customs Enforcement are the two most resented.

             More From WSJ   • Back in 2021, Chinese EV maker Skyworth Auto said its main EV plant could make 100,000 vehicles a year. Its actual sales in China this year through September: 660.

   • In his postmeeting press conference, Warsh hinted at how the trajectory of the AI boom —and the extent to which economic growth has broadened beyond it—will determine how high rates eventually go, Nick Timiraos writes.

   • The World Series has shown that in America, money doesn’t always buy you success. As the Yankees, Mets and Dodgers watch from the sidelines , the Brewers—with Major League Baseball’s 19th-largest payroll— just eliminated the Rays, with the 28th largest.

       What to Watch   Thursday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: Economists expect that the U.S. economy grew at an annualized 3.1% in the third quarter, an acceleration from 2.2% in the previous quarter. Annual core PCE inflation was probably 3.1% in September, per forecasters. 

   Friday 

   • Marco Rubio hosts a meeting of the G-20 foreign ministers in Atlanta.

   • Dissenting Fed voters often release a Friday statement explaining their vote. Look for messages from Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack.

   Monday 

   • 10 a.m. ET: The ISM publishes its October purchasing managers index for manufacturing. The previous monthly report showed a solid expansion.

   Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me . 

       What I’m Reading   • Caught between AI’s threat to hospitality jobs and its boost to construction, Nevada Teamsters are supporting candidates who would welcome data centers on tougher terms and shield workers from AI. ( Reuters )

   • The Walton family’s transformative philanthropic efforts have brought new highs and lows to life in Northwest Arkansas: new museums, schools and parks, but also traffic jams and higher rents. ( The New York Times )

   • The work of this years’ Nobel winners in economics shows why the Fed shouldn’t eliminate forward guidance, former Fed governor Alan Blinder argues. ( WSJ Opinion )
